title: What Does It Mean to Be an AI-Ready Lawyer? Farrah Pepper and Kirsten Talmage on AI Competency — full episode transcript
pub: AI and the Future of Law / 2030 Vision, American Arbitration Association
author: Farrah Pepper · Kirsten Talmage

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Associate training: Automation threatens expertise reproduction
st.an: Pepper shows that law students are gaining early access to generative AI and may use it in educational and career decisions, but she does not address whether automation undermines apprenticeship, creates a verification-experience paradox, or requires reconstructed associate training.
qs: What not everyone knows is that, just like back in the day you would get a Westlaw or Lexis license so you could do research, a lot of students are getting exposed very early on to generative AI.
And then there’s also just a lot that I would probably deploy it on as I was doing things as simple as picking my course schedule and figuring out what my daily life would look like.

st.t: Service redesign: Resistance reflects incentives and identity
st.an: The source accepts that AI adoption requires organisational change beyond acquiring tools and materially extends the cluster with an adaptable competency framework for diagnosing individual and firm-wide gaps, aligning training with organisational value and capabilities, and implementing priorities incrementally. Its claimed benefits remain early and largely unmeasured.
qs: Or for somebody who is responsible for the training or who heads innovation at a firm to take it and overlay it on top of the firm, to assess weaknesses and strengths and see where they perhaps need to spend more of their time with their attorneys.

It’s to show people what the end state can look like, but you have to put it through your own filter, your own priorities, where value is going to exist for your organization, where you’re weakest, where you’re strongest, and then tackle a little bit at a time.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source accepts selective, human-led AI deployment and materially extends the cluster by offering a cross-setting, multidimensional AI-fluency framework for developing user capability, alongside an experimental agentic workflow that accelerates rote production while preserving expert review and rewriting.
qs: We really evolved this competency framework to be something that could be applied whether you were in a law school setting, a law firm setting, or a legal group within an organization, so that it could be this shared language about what having AI fluency really means.
Look through them, review them, put them in your own words.”  But we’ve done a lot of that work that would take the constant back-and-forth over the six- to nine-month period.

st.t: Justice capacity: AI potential requires deliberate implementation
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s deliberate-implementation and professional-readiness agenda by encouraging organizations to deploy the competency framework, provide feedback and improve it iteratively. It offers an implementation practice rather than evidence that the framework improves access to justice or service outcomes.
qs: Farrah Pepper: Well, and Kirsten, we didn’t explicitly say this, but I think it’s implied that if anyone is listening to this, and you review what you see in the framework and you have strong views — you either think something should be different, or you want to actually bring it inside your organization and deploy it — reach out.

st.t: Practitioner engagement: Redesign should precede technological certainty
st.an: The source supports practitioner-led experimentation before technological certainty. It describes AI as a human-directed aid in everyday preparation and argues that rapidly changing capabilities make conventional educational planning cycles impractical. Its claims remain experiential and predictive, and the announced competency framework is not substantively explained.
qs: Bridget, this conversation is making me think of when we were teaching a class together in law school about AI, and how difficult it could be because every time we got together to plan for a fall class six months away, we just gave up because everything would be different by then.

st.t: Professional engagement: Lawyers should shape AI deployment
st.an: The source endorses active professional and organisational engagement with AI by inviting critique, collaboration and deployment of an AI competency framework. Its ongoing feedback process also supports deliberate learning and iterative implementation, though it provides no evidence that the framework is effective.

kp.k: Shared competency language addresses inconsistent legal AI training
kp.d: Kirsten Talmage says the framework arose from a late-fall 2025 workshop identifying inconsistent understandings of AI competency across lawyers and firms. PLI’s Innovation Council, the Professional Development Consortium board and Creative Lawyers subsequently developed it through workshops and feedback, intending a common language usable in law schools, law firms and corporate legal groups.
qs: These three entities came together based on a workshop that was held in the late fall of 2025.
And the one thing that resonated throughout that group was a lack of a shared understanding of what AI competency or AI fluency means, not just for individual attorneys but also for law firms.
What they were seeing was that attorneys would go from one firm to another with very different understandings of what it meant to have competency in AI.

kp.k: Proficiency is multidimensional rather than a single certification
kp.d: Talmage describes five pillars and three proficiency levels, deliberately without certification or a linear progression across pillars. The transcript is internally inconsistent about the competency count: her initial description says 20 under each pillar, whereas later statements describe 20 competencies overall. Lawyers can have different proficiency levels in different areas.
qs: In the end, what it is is a framework that has five pillars. It has 20 competencies under each of those pillars, and it has three levels of proficiency.
And when we were making it, we very intentionally did not attach a certification to it. There’s no linearity. You can be fluent in one of the pillars and lacking fluency in another.
So similarly, in this framework, there are 20 competencies.

kp.k: AI competence includes application, verification, ethics and governance
kp.d: Talmage describes understanding tools, integrating them into existing workflows, checking their outputs for hallucinations and preserving attorney judgment, alongside ethical and governance awareness. Her account explicitly frames AI as augmentation rather than replacement; the discussion does not separately enumerate all five pillars.
qs: The first pillar is AI fluency: do you understand what the tools are? Do you understand how to use the tools?
Not can you use the tool in an AI-first fashion, but as an enhancement.
Because the third pillar actually goes right along with that second pillar, and that is making sure that what AI produces to enhance your work — not replace it — is actually the right thing.
So, ensuring that there aren’t any hallucinations, that there isn’t anything that wouldn’t be what you would produce as an attorney with judgment and skill.

And then, of course, there’s the governance piece that goes on top of it, and ensuring that all attorneys understand the ethical implications of using AI in their daily workflows or as a thought partner.

kp.k: Framework seeks durable, adaptable standards across training providers
kp.d: Talmage says the framework is intended to evolve without depending on particular tools or innovations. Pepper hopes vendor education, including Harvey Academy, will align with a discipline-wide vocabulary so lawyers’ development remains intelligible across providers. This is an aspiration for future alignment, not a report of completed mapping.
qs: It is ever-evolving as things change, as they are changing every week, it seems like at this point.
We can evolve the framework, but it is also not tool-specific. It is also not innovation-specific.
Because if you get a certification inside of Harvey Academy and a proficiency level inside of the PLI framework, the idea is that’s actually describing the same growth.
And we don’t want a lawyer or a legal professional’s development to be trapped inside of any one vocabulary.
I’m hoping that going forward, as materials are created, there will be that alignment so that we don’t have death by a thousand training certifications.

kp.k: E-discovery provides an analogy for common AI standards
kp.d: Pepper compares the framework’s intended function with the EDRM model’s role in establishing shared e-discovery terminology and workflows. She treats this as a historical analogy and aspiration: industry experts can make training and communication possible through a common reference, although the two frameworks concern different subjects.
qs: There was no shared lingo. There were no predefined workflows.
So the parallel that struck me is that this framework is very similar to the EDRM model in kindred-spirit ways, meaning they touch on completely different things.

And so the hope and aspiration that I have for the AI Ready Lawyer framework is that it becomes what EDRM was to e-discovery: a common way of looking at things, thinking about things, and talking and teaching about things.

kp.k: Training audits should guide incremental, organization-specific implementation
kp.d: Talmage recommends mapping existing training against competencies, identifying gaps and selecting internal or external resources appropriate to organizational needs and capacity. She reports that PLI applied this process to its own catalog and is producing programs to address gaps. Pepper cautions against tackling all competencies simultaneously, recommending prioritization by organizational value, strengths and weaknesses.
qs: We found some gaps, and we’re currently producing programs to fill those gaps.
I would actually recommend doing exactly what we did at PLI, which is first, an audit of your current content.
Because if you’re sitting in an Am Law 200 firm versus a midsize firm, you’re going to have very different needs and resources available to you.

It’s to show people what the end state can look like, but you have to put it through your own filter, your own priorities, where value is going to exist for your organization, where you’re weakest, where you’re strongest, and then tackle a little bit at a time.

kp.k: Early feedback suggests demand from resource-constrained firms
kp.d: Talmage reports hearing from, in her qualified recollection, over 35 law firms during the first week after release, spanning Am Law 200 firms through smaller specialist firms. She describes particularly positive feedback from midsize firms lacking larger firms’ innovation staff and resources. This is reported early feedback, not measured adoption or evidence of improved competency.
qs: Within the first week of its release, we heard from, I think it was, over 35 law firms just spanning the gamut — so Am Law 200 all the way down to smaller firms that have specializations in specific areas.
And what we’re seeing is it’s been particularly needed and in play in midsize firms, because as I alluded to earlier, they don’t have the same resources and staffing that the Am Law 200 firms have.
They don’t have a director or a chief innovation officer. They don’t have access to the same tools that the larger firms have.

kp.k: Smaller in-house teams may especially benefit from shared resources
kp.d: Pepper argues that resource-constrained smaller legal teams may benefit disproportionately from AI and the framework. Based on her in-house experience, she says dedicated legal learning resources are uncommon even in large departments, leaving teams dependent on law firms and external educators. Talmage confirms the framework is freely downloadable without membership, supporting its intended use by individuals as well as organizations.
qs: And one thing that’s interesting to me is that smaller teams can actually benefit from AI more because they are so resource-constrained, and similarly, may actually benefit more from this framework because it is the rare large legal department that actually has in-house training, development, and learning resources.
But most often, in-house teams of every size are relying heavily on law firms and groups like PLI to give them the education that they need.
You do not. It is free to download. Anybody can download it.

kp.k: Experimental agents accelerate educational asset production
kp.d: Talmage reports that PLI is experimenting with orchestrated agents to prepare program assets for volunteer speakers to review and adapt. She contrasts a six- to nine-month program-planning process with 15 minutes to an hour for asset creation; this does not establish that the entire program-production cycle now takes that time. She says the approach removes rote work and better uses human expertise, while easier speaker recruitment remains a hope rather than a demonstrated outcome.
qs: It takes about a six- to nine-month planning period to plan these programs.
We’ve reduced the actual time to create those assets to 15 minutes to an hour, and it gets us off to a running start.

And I should say this is in the experimentation phase still, but it’s been very interesting to build these agents that can really do a lot of this work for us and take a lot of the burden off of our speakers, who are all volunteers.
And it allows us to use our human experts to the highest of their capabilities. So it removes that rote work as well.

kp.k: AI preparation tools preserve human authorship while saving time
kp.d: Pepper describes using generative AI to format presentation materials and challenge her ideas through anticipated questions, while retaining responsibility for substance and voice. She reports substantial but unquantified time savings from this personal workflow; it is an example of augmentation, not a controlled productivity finding.
qs: I want it to have my voice.

And so my Aha! has been leveraging generative AI as a thought partner and as a style designer, so that as I go into different sessions, I can do the part that I love, which is thinking through what I want to convey and how I want to do it, and have this partner who will basically take things like slide formats and do a lot of the messy work to shape my ideas.

And then once I put together something that I feel good about initially, which takes a fraction of the time that it used to as a cumbersome human working alone, I then also use it as a sparring partner to try to think about what might be the hardest or most interesting questions I would get, and to be ready for that.

kp.k: Emerging hybrid roles make competencies more important than titles
kp.d: McCormack reports hiring for newly invented roles spanning technology and the general counsel’s office. Pepper describes moving between law firms, in-house practice and a legal-tech company as acquiring complementary perspectives that improve judgment. Her expectation of additional new roles is an optimistic prediction based on personal experience, not a labor-market finding.
qs: We’re hiring people now in these roles that we’re just making up titles for because they didn’t exist six months ago or a year ago. They’re straddling tech and the GC’s office in-house in my organization, so we’re just making up job titles.
And I’m seeing law firms, in-house, and tech companies not really as three different careers anymore. They’re three different vantage points, three different perspectives.
And the more you see of each of them, the better your judgment gets — just your legal judgment. That’s been my experience thus far.
my job that I’m in now didn’t exist five months ago, and there’s going to be plenty more that didn’t exist five months from today.

kp.k: Students can assess educational and employer AI readiness
kp.d: Talmage recommends using the framework to compare accepted law schools’ AI programs and training. Pepper suggests students use available AI tools to examine whether prospective employers’ practices match their claims. Leonard adds that students can use framework gaps to advocate for curricular changes. These are proposed uses, not reported student outcomes.
qs: So you could take the framework and apply it to the programs and training that the law schools offer in the areas of AI and innovation.

One that immediately springs to mind is thinking about future employers and doing an assessment of what people say they do in terms of leveraging AI, and comparing that to what they’re actually doing — whether the talk and the walk meet as you’re selecting where you want to spend your future.
So when they discover that not everything in the framework is on their course schedule or available to them, they can advocate for change from their own perspective and position, which I love.

kp.k: Familiarity with AI may erode ethical vigilance
kp.d: Talmage warns that students accustomed to AI could become complacent about professional obligations. She recommends continuing attention to ethics and governance from law school into practice and preserving AI’s role as a thought partner rather than a replacement for either lawyers or students. This is a prospective risk assessment, not evidence of observed ethical deterioration.
qs: And I think there is the risk of complacency and familiarity there that sort of loses the ethical obligations that we, as attorneys, need to keep in mind.
So I think using the framework in that manner throughout your life cycle — from being a law student into your practice, when you pass the bar and become an attorney — is really important.
And I think that goes also to using AI as a thought partner and not a replacer for an attorney, and for a law student as well.

kp.k: Assessments and tailored training remain under development
kp.d: Talmage says PLI is experimenting with an assessment to identify individual strengths and weaknesses and potentially recommend training. Certification has been discussed but is not presented as available; any future approach would need to preserve the framework’s nonlinearity.
qs: Right now, we’re in the experimentation phase with a few things. One is an assessment
We could recommend trainings based on those areas of strengths and weaknesses.
And then certification is something that we have tossed around.

We have CLE, and that’s been our main focus, but certainly there is something around the certification without creating the linearity in the framework, because that’s something we really want to avoid.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Pepper reports that generative AI substantially accelerates presentation preparation while preserving her authorship and supporting rehearsal.
pts.d: Farrah Pepper describes using AI to format and shape her ideas and anticipate challenging audience questions. This is an account of augmentation in her own professional workflow, not a measured claim about legal-service productivity.

pts.k: Talmage reports experimental agent-based acceleration of legal-education asset production.
pts.d: Kirsten Talmage says PLI is building orchestrated agents to prepare program assets in 15 minutes to an hour, reducing preparation burdens on volunteer speakers. The six-to-nine-month comparator describes the overall program-planning period; she does not establish that the entire planning process now takes 15 minutes to an hour.

pts.k: Pepper sees increasingly connected career paths across law firms, corporate legal departments and legal-tech companies, and predicts additional new roles.
pts.d: Pepper draws on her move from Marsh to Harvey, the legal-AI company, and her earlier Big Law experience. She says exposure to different professional settings improves her legal judgment and anticipates more newly created jobs. This is personal experience and an optimistic prediction, not a quantified employment forecast.

pts.k: Talmage and Pepper argue that AI adoption requires a shared, portable vocabulary for professional competence.
pts.d: Talmage says inconsistent understandings of AI competence across firms motivated the framework. Pepper hopes it will play a coordinating role analogous to EDRM in e-discovery and enable alignment across education providers, including Harvey Academy. Alignment is an aspiration, not an announced completed integration.

pts.k: Talmage frames AI competence as augmentation coupled with human verification, judgment and ethical governance.
pts.d: Talmage describes understanding tools, applying them to workflows, checking their outputs and understanding ethical implications. Her framing keeps the lawyer responsible rather than endorsing autonomous substitution. She also predicts that increasing familiarity with AI may create complacency about professional obligations.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The productivity and career claims rest on participants’ experience and internal experimentation.
pts.d: Pepper supplies personal workflow observations and experience across professional settings, including only four months at Harvey. Talmage supplies internally reported production times from an experimental PLI workflow. No controlled productivity study, independent benchmark or labor-market dataset is offered.

pts.k: Evidence for the framework’s usefulness consists of collaborative development, an internal curriculum audit and early reported firm feedback.
pts.d: Talmage describes workshops involving PLI’s Innovation Council, the Professional Development Consortium board and Creative Lawyers. PLI’s audit identified training gaps. She reports contact from over 35 firms during the first release week, with particularly positive responses from midsize firms. These are reports of need and reception, not measured improvements in lawyer proficiency or legal outcomes.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The episode distinguishes current experiments and early experience from future expectations.
pts.d: In this 2026 source, the framework follows a late-fall-2025 workshop and its reception is described using first-week feedback. PLI’s agent workflow remains experimental; speakers still review and personalize generated assets. Easier speaker recruitment is an expectation rather than an established result. Pepper’s new-role prediction points to the next five months.

pts.k: The framework is intended to evolve, be applied selectively and avoid a single linear certification pathway.
pts.d: Talmage describes a tool-independent framework whose proficiency levels may differ by pillar. Pepper recommends incremental implementation based on organizational priorities and resources. Assessments and training recommendations are being explored, while certification is only under discussion. The transcript initially describes 20 competencies under each pillar but subsequently repeatedly refers to 20 competencies overall; this inconsistency should not be silently resolved as 100 competencies.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: Midsize firms and smaller in-house teams are presented as especially likely to benefit from shared training resources and AI augmentation.
pts.d: Talmage says midsize firms often lack the staffing and tools available to larger firms and are using the framework to structure training. Pepper says resource constraints may make AI and the framework particularly valuable to smaller corporate legal teams, while in-house teams of all sizes rely on external education. These are resource-based claims, not quantified comparative benefits.

pts.k: Individual lawyers, training leaders, law students and prospective students can use the framework to identify gaps and inform choices.
pts.d: Talmage presents the framework as usable both by individuals, including small-firm and solo practitioners, and by organizational training leaders. She proposes assessing law schools’ AI readiness. Pepper suggests students could use AI to compare prospective employers’ claims with their actual adoption practices. These student applications are proposed uses rather than documented results. Free access removes a subscription requirement for the framework itself.
